title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Seventeen officers in all were riding in this race. The course was a large three-mile elliptical ring in front of the pavilion. Nine obstacles had been laid out on it: the stream; a big, solid barrier five feet high just in front of the pavilion; a dry ditch; a ditch full of water; a steep slope; an Irish barricade (one of the hardest obstacles, consisting of a mound fenced with brushwood, beyond which was a ditch hidden from the horses, so that the horse had to clear both at once or risk a fatal fall); then two more water-filled ditches and one dry one; and the finish was directly opposite the pavilion. But the race began not in the ring but two hundred yards out from it, and in that stretch of the course was the first obstacle, a dammed-up stream seven feet across, which the racers could leap or wade through, as they preferred.

Three times they were lined up to start, and each time one horse or another broke from the line, and they had to begin again. The starter, Colonel Sestrin, was starting to lose his temper, when at last for the fourth time he shouted "Away!" and the racers were off.
Every eye, every opera-glass, was turned on the brightly colored cluster of riders at the moment they were in line to start.
"They're off! They're starting!" went up on all sides after the hush of expectation.

And small groups and lone figures in the public began running from place to place to get a better view. In the very first moment the tight bunch of horsemen drew apart, and you could see them approaching the stream in twos and threes, one behind another. To the spectators it looked as if they had all started at the same instant, but for the racers there were seconds of difference that mattered a great deal.

Frou-Frou, jumpy and over-nervous, had missed the first moment, and several horses had started before her, but before reaching the stream Vronsky, holding the mare in with all his strength as she tugged at the bridle, easily overtook three of them, and was left with Mahotin's chestnut Gladiator in front of him, whose hindquarters were moving lightly and rhythmically up and down right ahead of Vronsky, and in front of all the dainty mare Diana carrying Kuzovlev more dead than alive.
For the first instant Vronsky was master neither of himself nor of his mare. Up to the first obstacle, the stream, he could not control her movements.

Gladiator and Diana came up to it together and almost at the same instant; together they rose above the stream and flew to the other side; Frou-Frou shot after them as if airborne; but at the very moment Vronsky felt himself in the air, he suddenly saw, almost beneath his mare's hoofs, Kuzovlev floundering on the far side of the stream with Diana. (Kuzovlev had let go of the reins as he took the leap, and the mare had thrown him over her head.) Vronsky learned the details later; at that moment all he saw was that, just below him, where Frou-Frou had to land, Diana's legs or head might be in the way. But Frou-Frou drew up her legs and back in the very act of jumping, like a falling cat, and, clearing the other mare, landed beyond her.
"Oh, the darling!" Vronsky thought.

After crossing the stream Vronsky had complete control of his mare and began holding her in, meaning to clear the big barrier behind Mahotin and to try to overtake him on the open stretch of about five hundred yards that came next.

The big barrier stood right in front of the imperial pavilion. The Tsar and the whole court and crowds of people were all watching them — at him, with Mahotin a length ahead, as they approached the "devil," as the solid barrier was called. Vronsky was aware of those eyes fastened on him from every side, but he saw nothing except the ears and neck of his own mare, the ground racing to meet him, and the back and white legs of Gladiator beating time swiftly in front of him, always at the same distance ahead. Gladiator rose, with no sound of striking anything. With a flick of his short tail he vanished from Vronsky's sight.
"Bravo!" cried a voice.

At that same moment, just beneath Vronsky's eyes, the palings of the barrier flashed by. With no change in her stride his mare flew over it; the palings disappeared, and he heard only a crash behind him. The mare, excited by Gladiator keeping ahead, had risen too early before the barrier and grazed it with her hind hoofs. But her pace never broke, and Vronsky, feeling a spatter of mud strike his face, realized he was once again the same distance from Gladiator. Once more he saw before him the same back and short tail, and again the same swiftly moving white legs that got no further away.

At the very moment Vronsky was thinking now was the time to overtake Mahotin, Frou-Frou herself, picking up on his thoughts without any prompting from him, gained ground considerably and began coming alongside Mahotin on the most favorable side, close to the inner rope. Mahotin wouldn't let her by on that side. Vronsky had barely formed the thought that he might pass on the outer side, when Frou-Frou shifted her stride and began overtaking him on the other side. Frou-Frou's shoulder, by now beginning to darken with sweat, was level with Gladiator's back. For a few lengths they ran even. But before the next obstacle they were approaching, Vronsky began working the reins, eager to avoid being forced to the outer circle, and swiftly passed Mahotin just at the dip. He caught a glimpse of his mud-spattered face as he flashed by. He even fancied that Mahotin smiled. Vronsky passed Mahotin, but he was immediately aware of him close behind, never ceasing to hear the even thud of hoofs and the rapid, still entirely fresh breathing of Gladiator.

The next two obstacles, the water course and the barrier, were easily cleared, but Vronsky began to hear Gladiator's snort and thud closer behind him. He urged his mare on, and to his delight felt her easily quicken her pace, and the thud of Gladiator's hoofs was again at the same distance away.

Vronsky was at the head of the race, just as he had wanted to be and as Cord had advised, and now he felt sure of being the winner. His excitement, his joy, his tenderness for Frou-Frou grew sharper and sharper. He longed to look back, but he didn't dare, and he tried to keep cool and not push his mare, so as to leave the same reserve of strength in her that he sensed Gladiator still had. Only one obstacle remained, the hardest one; if he could clear it ahead of the others he would come in first. He was flying toward the Irish barricade. Frou-Frou and he both saw the barricade in the distance, and both man and mare had a moment's hesitation. He saw the uncertainty in the mare's ears and lifted the whip, but at the same time felt his fears were groundless; the mare knew what was wanted. She quickened her stride and rose smoothly, just as he had imagined she would, and as she left the ground she gave herself up to the force of her surge, which carried her far beyond the ditch; and with the same rhythm, without effort, with the same leading leg, Frou-Frou settled back into her stride.

"Bravo, Vronsky!" he heard shouts from a knot of men — he knew they were his friends from the regiment — standing by the obstacle. He could not fail to recognize Yashvin's voice, though he did not see him.

"Oh, my sweet!" he said inwardly to Frou-Frou, listening for what was happening behind him. "He's cleared it!" he thought, catching the thud of Gladiator's hoofs behind him. Only the last ditch remained, filled with water and five feet across. Vronsky didn't even look at it, but, eager to come in well ahead, he began sawing at the reins, lifting the mare's head and letting it go in time with her pace. He felt that the mare was at her last reserve of strength; not just her neck and shoulders were wet, but sweat stood in drops on her mane, her head, her sharp ears, and her breath came in short, sharp gasps. But he knew she had strength more than enough for the remaining five hundred yards. It was only from the sense of being closer to the ground, and the peculiar smoothness of his motion, that Vronsky knew how much the mare had quickened her pace. She flew over the ditch as if not noticing it. She flew over it like a bird; but in that same instant Vronsky, to his horror, felt that he had failed to keep up with the mare's motion — that he had, he could not say how, made a fearful, unforgivable mistake in recovering his seat in the saddle. All at once his position had shifted and he knew something terrible had happened. He couldn't yet make out what, when the white legs of a chestnut horse flashed by close to him, and Mahotin shot past at a swift gallop. Vronsky was touching the ground with one foot, and his mare was sinking onto that foot. He just had time to free his leg before she fell on one side, gasping painfully, and, making vain efforts to rise with her delicate, soaking neck, she fluttered on the ground at his feet like a shot bird. The clumsy movement Vronsky had made had broken her back. But that he only learned much later. At that moment all he knew was that Mahotin had flown swiftly past, while he stood staggering alone on the muddy, motionless ground, with Frou-Frou lying gasping in front of him, bending her head back and gazing at him with her exquisite eyes. Still unable to grasp what had happened, Vronsky tugged at his mare's reins. Again she struggled all over like a fish, and her shoulders heaving against the saddle, she rose onto her forelegs but, unable to lift her back, she shuddered and again fell on her side. With a face hideous with passion, his lower jaw shaking and his cheeks white, Vronsky kicked her with his heel in the stomach and again tugged at the reins. She did not stir, but, thrusting her nose into the ground, simply gazed at her master with her speaking eyes.
"A-a-ah!" Vronsky groaned, clutching at his head. "Ah, what have I done!" he cried. "The race lost! And my fault! Shameful, unforgivable! And the poor darling, ruined mare! Ah — what have I done!"

A crowd of men, a doctor and his assistant, the officers of his regiment, ran up to him. To his misery he felt that he was whole and unhurt. The mare had broken her back, and it was decided to shoot her. Vronsky could not answer questions, could not speak to anyone. He turned, and, without picking up his cap that had fallen off, walked away from the racecourse with no idea where he was going. He felt utterly wretched. For the first time in his life he had come to know the bitterest sort of misfortune — misfortune past mending, and caused by his own fault.

Yashvin caught up with him with his cap, and led him home; and half an hour later Vronsky had pulled himself together. But the memory of that race stayed in his heart for a long time, the cruelest and bitterest memory of his life.
